title: Linear Transformations and Matrices: A Visual Introduction

sections.title: The Basis Vectors
sections.teaches: Understanding the standard basis vectors i-hat and j-hat as the foundation of the coordinate system.
sections.visual: A 2D Cartesian grid appears. The unit vector i-hat (red) points to (1,0) and j-hat (blue) points to (0,1). Labels 'i' and 'j' appear next to them. The vectors remain stationary while the grid lines subtly pulse.
sections.narration: Before we transform anything, let's define our reference frame. In standard 2D space, every point is built from two fundamental directions: i-hat along the x-axis and j-hat along the y-axis.

sections.title: Transforming the Basis
sections.teaches: A linear transformation is fully defined by where it moves the basis vectors.
sections.visual: The grid warps smoothly. The red i-hat rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise to point up, and the blue j-hat rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise to point left. The entire grid stretches and rotates with them, maintaining parallel lines.
sections.narration: A linear transformation reshapes the space itself. Notice how the grid moves rigidly: if we know where i-hat and j-hat land, we know exactly where every other point in the universe goes.

sections.title: From Vectors to Columns
sections.teaches: The new positions of the basis vectors form the columns of the transformation matrix.
sections.visual: The transformed i-hat (now at 0,1) and j-hat (now at -1,0) are highlighted. Two brackets appear around them, forming a 2x2 matrix: [[0, -1], [1, 0]]. The numbers inside the matrix pulse in sync with the vector tips.
sections.narration: This is the magic trick: the destination of i-hat becomes the first column of our matrix, and the destination of j-hat becomes the second column. The matrix is simply a record of where the basis vectors ended up.

sections.title: Matrix-Vector Multiplication
sections.teaches: Multiplying a matrix by a vector computes the new position using linear combination.
sections.visual: A green point at (2,1) appears. It moves to (-1, 2). An equation appears: [[0, -1], [1, 0]] * [2, 1] = [-1, 2]. The calculation breaks down visually: 2 times the first column plus 1 times the second column equals the final position.
sections.narration: To find where any point goes, we multiply the matrix by its coordinates. This operation is a linear combination: we scale the new basis vectors by the original coordinates and add them together to find the final destination.
